{{Other people|John Brownlee}}
'''John Brownlee''' (1868–1927) was a British physician and [[medical statistics|medical statistician]] who became the first director of the Statistics Department of the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|UK's Medical Research Committee]].<ref name="pmid16755605">{{cite journal|vauthors=Farewell V, Johnson T, Armitage P | title='A memorandum on the Present Position and Prospects of Medical Statistics and Epidemiology' by Major Greenwood. | journal=Stat Med | year= 2006 | volume= 25 | issue= 13 | pages= 2161–77 | pmid=16755605 | doi=10.1002/sim.2608 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Life==
The son of a [[Church of Scotland]] minister, he studied at the [[University of Glasgow]], obtaining degrees first in mathematics and [[natural philosophy]] and then in medicine. He became in 1900 physician-superintendent to the [[City of Glasgow Fever and Smallpox Hospitals, Belvidere|City of Glasgow Fever Hospital]] and the new [[Ruchill Hospital]] from 1908.<ref name=BMJ>[http://www.bmj.com/content/1/3455/598.1.extract ''BMJ Obituary'']</ref><ref>{{cite journal | pmc = 407360 | page=749 | volume=17 | issue=6 | journal=Can Med Assoc J | title=Dr. Richard R. Hopkins| year=1927 }}</ref> In 1914 he became the founding director of the statistics department of the [[Medical Research Council (UK)|UK Medical Research Committee]] and held the post until his sudden death from [[bronchopneumonia]] in 1927.<ref>{{cite journal|author=George Davey Smith |url=http://ije.oxfordjournals.org/content/37/5/911.full |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120709031039/http://ije.oxfordjournals.org/content/37/5/911.full |url-status=dead |archive-date=2012-07-09 |title=How do we know, what do we know and what can knowledge do? From John Brownlee to translational medicine |journal=[[International Journal of Epidemiology]] |date=2011-04-02 |access-date=2011-07-29|author-link=George Davey Smith }}</ref>

==Works==
Brownlee was influenced by [[Karl Pearson]]'s mathematical approach to statistics, and applied the [[Pearson distribution|Pearson family of distributions]] to [[epidemic]]s. In the view of fellow epidemiologist and statistician [[Major Greenwood]], Brownlee took these techniques further than any of his contemporaries.<ref>[http://www.economics.soton.ac.uk/staff/aldrich/Hardy%20and%20Magnello.pdf, p. 6 of PDF.]{{doi|10.1007/BF01318387}}</ref> His studies included the epidemiology of [[Tuberculosis|phthisis]] and [[measles]].<ref name=BMJ/>
